findings.source_passage: "But I am not a brave man; never said I was a brave man; I am a coward; and I sing to keep up my spirits. And I tell you what it is, Mr. Starbuck, there's no way to stop my singing in this world but to cut my throat. And when that's done, ten to one I sing ye the doxology for a wind-up."
findings.why_it_matters: The full speech — including the specific 'doxology for a wind-up' line — is a signature Stubb moment widely cited for his comic defiance in the face of death. The draft collapses it to a fragment, losing the rhetorical escalation and the final punchline entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full Stubb speech verbatim or near-verbatim, particularly 'there's no way to stop my singing in this world but to cut my throat. And when that's done, ten to one I sing ye the doxology for a wind-up.'

findings.source_passage: "Madman! look through my eyes if thou hast none of thine own." "What! how can you see better of a dark night than anybody else, never mind how foolish?"
findings.source_locator: exchange between Starbuck and Stubb, after Stubb's coward speech
findings.why_it_matters: This exchange is a critically noted moment of grotesque comedy cutting against Starbuck's prophetic urgency; its erasure removes a key tonal pivot that critics read as deliberate deflation before Starbuck's omen speech.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore both lines verbatim; they are short and carry heavy dramatic and comic weight.

findings.source_passage: in all my voyagings, seldom have I heard a common oath when God's burning finger has been laid on the ship; when His "Mene, Mene, Tekel Upharsin" has been woven into the shrouds and the cordage.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'To sailors, oaths are household words'
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of the most critically cited biblical allusions in the chapter — 'Mene, Mene, Tekel Upharsin' woven into the rigging — used by scholars to decode the doom-writing symbolism of the corpusants. Its complete absence is a serious interpretive loss.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full paragraph, especially the 'Mene, Mene, Tekel Upharsin' sentence verbatim.

findings.source_passage: "Oh! thou clear spirit of clear fire … I now know thee, thou clear spirit, and I now know that thy right worship is defiance … In the midst of the personified impersonal, a personality stands here … the queenly personality lives in me, and feels her royal rights. But war is pain, and hate is woe. Come in thy lowest form of love, and I will kneel and kiss thee; but at thy highest, come as mere supernal power; and though thou launchest navies of full-freighted worlds, there's that in here that still remains indifferent."
findings.source_locator: Ahab's first great speech to the fire
findings.why_it_matters: The draft uses ellipses to skip 'war is pain, and hate is woe' and the entire 'Come in thy lowest form of love … there's that in here that still remains indifferent' passage — among the most famous and most critically interpreted lines in Melville, central to debates about Ahab's gnosticism and defiance-as-worship.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim: 'But war is pain, and hate is woe. Come in thy lowest form of love, and I will kneel and kiss thee; but at thy highest, come as mere supernal power; and though thou launchest navies of full-freighted worlds, there's that in here that still remains indifferent.'

findings.source_passage: "I know that of me, which thou knowest not of thyself, oh, thou omnipotent. There is some unsuffusing thing beyond thee, thou clear spirit, to whom all thy eternity is but time, all thy creativeness mechanical."
findings.why_it_matters: This passage — 'some unsuffusing thing beyond thee … all thy creativeness mechanical' — is one of the most discussed theological statements in American literature, key to readings of Melville's gnosticism and Ahab's metaphysics. Its complete absence is a severe interpretive loss.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim from 'I know that of me, which thou knowest not of thyself' through 'all thy creativeness mechanical.'

findings.source_passage: "Yes, yes, round the Cape of Good Hope is the shortest way to Nantucket," soliloquized Starbuck suddenly, heedless of Stubb's question. "The gale that now hammers at us to stave us, we can turn it into a fair wind … Yonder, to windward, all is blackness of doom; but to leeward, homeward—I see it lightens up there; but not with the lightning."
findings.source_locator: Starbuck's soliloquy after pointing out the omen
findings.why_it_matters: The soliloquy's closing line — 'but not with the lightning' — is a signature phrase that critics treat as Starbuck's most poetic moment; it is compressed away, and the 'Cape of Good Hope' opening, signalling his only real temptation to mutiny, is reduced to a vague 'lightens to leeward.'
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the soliloquy with 'round the Cape of Good Hope is the shortest way to Nantucket' and 'to leeward, homeward—I see it lightens up there; but not with the lightning' preserved verbatim.

findings.source_passage: "But I am not a brave man … I take that mast-head flame we saw for a sign of good luck … and so, all that sperm will work up into the masts, like sap in a tree. Yes, our three masts will yet be as three spermaceti candles—that's the good promise we saw."
findings.source_locator: Stubb's speech to Starbuck after the first waning of corpusants
findings.why_it_matters: The full speech with the 'sap in a tree' analogy and its unconscious irony (the candles = the chapter title) is compressed to bare summary, losing Melville's deliberate title-echo and the ironic self-delusion that characterises Stubb's voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'all that sperm will work up into the masts, like sap in a tree. Yes, our three masts will yet be as three spermaceti candles—that's the good promise we saw' verbatim.

findings.source_passage: "Avast!" cried Ahab; "let's have fair play here, though we be the weaker side. Yet I'll contribute to raise rods on the Himmalehs and Andes, that all the world may be secured; but out on privileges! Let them be, sir."
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'let's have fair play here, though we be the weaker side' establishes Ahab's defiance of divine protection as a point of personal honour, not mere recklessness; the draft drops this opening clause, losing the rhetorical framing.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full speech beginning 'let's have fair play here, though we be the weaker side' before the Himmalehs line.

summary: The draft commits multiple high-severity losses including: the complete excision of the 'Mene, Mene, Tekel Upharsin' passage, the 'there's that in here that still remains indifferent' clause of Ahab's fire-speech, and the 'some unsuffusing thing beyond thee … all thy creativeness mechanical' passage — among the most critically discussed lines in the chapter — plus heavy flattening of Stubb's coward speech, the 'Madman' exchange, and Starbuck's soliloquy.
